source.title: A Probabilistic Representation of Deep Learning

record.tranche_reason: Compares natural-label and random-label generalization with CNNs on a synthetic dataset, using a different setting from V1.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for synthetic labels and random labels. The random-label CNN results and the natural-label CNN comparison bear on V1; cited findings from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests random-label memorization alongside structured-label generalization (V1), and compares test error at two widths that both achieve zero training error (V2), in a new synthetic-image setting.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' account, but omits a central distinction: they call accurate input-prior estimation good generalization even under random labels, despite poor held-out classification. They argue that learning a prior provides explicit regularization and that the relaxed backpropagation objective can impair prior estimation. These are their proposed explanations, not mechanisms independently established by the classification comparisons.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a synthetic Gaussian image dataset and two CNN architectures; the optimizer, batch size, and training recipe are not stated. The natural-label and random-label experiments are not on the named benchmark datasets in V1.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported natural-label generalization differs between CNN1 and CNN2, which have different numbers of convolutional filters in one layer.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors compare estimated input-prior distributions, including KL distances of 0.94 for CNN1 and 1.59 for CNN2, and report accurate prior estimation under random labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hidden-layer distribution estimates can approximate the input distribution, including after random-label training.

record.problems: The evidence uses a synthetic dataset and only two CNN architectures. Testing-error values are presented in plots without numerical values in the text, and uncertainty estimates are not stated. The claim that DNNs cannot classify random labels conflicts with the reported zero training error on random labels; the paper's toy explanation does not resolve that discrepancy for the CNN experiment.

untested.parts: The named benchmark datasets and architectures; verified matching training recipes without explicit regularization; quantitative above-chance structured-label accuracy and chance-level random-label accuracy.

The original one-hidden-layer fully connected setting, training to convergence without explicit regularization, identification of the minimum interpolating width, and continued improvement across a wider range of widths.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or generalization-gap ranking.
No removal and retraining experiment involving memorized examples.

missing.what: CNN2 also achieves zero training error on the structured-label dataset. Record this separately because it establishes that both widths interpolate for the V2 comparison.
Readable final test-error values for both structured-label CNNs and random-label CNN1 are needed to quantify the width comparison and assess the chance-level component.

record.verdict_notes: The CNN1–CNN2 difference does not justify a V1 limits_scope verdict: V1 does not require identical generalization across architectures. The authors' statement about inability to classify random labels concerns held-out prediction in context; their experiment explicitly demonstrates fitting random training labels. Numerical curves are not recoverable from the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: The named CIFAR-10 and ImageNet models and datasets, the specific architectures in the version, and the cited Zhang et al. setting are not tested.
